hook: You know God tested Abraham with his son Isaac. But did you know the King James Bible says God did tempt him, while James says God tempts no one?
story:
The chapter opens with a line that tells the reader something Abraham himself is never told: “After these things, God tested Abraham”. Then the command comes: “Now take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love”, and offer him “as a burnt offering”. “Abraham rose early in the morning”. On the way the boy asks, “where is the lamb for a burnt offering?” His father answers, “God will provide himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” On the mountain Abraham takes the knife, and the LORD’s angel calls out of the sky: “Don’t lay your hand on the boy”.

Now turn to the letter of James. It warns that no one should say he is tempted by God, “for God can’t be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.”

In the World English Bible the two verses do not collide. God tests, and God tempts no one. But open the King James Bible of 1611 and they do. There Genesis says that God did tempt Abraham, and James says that God tempts no man.

The clash is not only an English one. The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures that the early church used, tells Genesis 22:1 with the verb peirazo, to test or to tempt. James 1:13 uses that same verb for the tempting that God never does.

So the question is fair. Does God tempt people, or does he not?

moment:
Genesis says this came “After these things”, and the things had taken a lifetime. “Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran.” The son he was promised came twenty-five years later: “Abraham was one hundred years old when his son, Isaac, was born to him.” Sarah said, “God has made me laugh.”

Then the household broke apart. Sarah demanded that Hagar and her son be sent away, and Genesis names what Abraham felt: “The thing was very grievous in Abraham’s sight on account of his son.” God told him to let them go, with a promise: “For your offspring will be named through Isaac.”

So the son God now asks for is the son on whom every promise rests. This time Genesis does not say what Abraham felt. It says only what he did. He rose early, split the wood and walked for three days. To his servants he said, “We will worship, and come back to you.” Whether that was faith, hope or only words, the text leaves open. The letter to the Hebrews later read it as faith: Abraham was “concluding that God is able to raise up even from the dead.”
around:
Right after the test, the angel says what it showed: “For now I know that you fear God”. Abraham names the place “The LORD Will Provide”.

The verse in James has its own surroundings, and they matter. A few verses earlier James writes, “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance.” In verse 12 he adds, “Blessed is a person who endures temptation”. Then he turns: “each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed.”

In the Greek, the trials James calls a joy and the tempting he says God never does are named with words from one root, the noun peirasmos and the verb peirazo. Thayer’s lexicon on Bible Hub lists James 1:2 among the troubles sent by God to prove a person’s faith, and James 1:13 under the enticement to sin. James uses one family of words for two different things within a dozen verses.
after:
Isaac lived. Genesis ends the scene briefly: “So Abraham returned to his young men”, and they went together to Beersheba, where Abraham lived. The name of the land comes back only once more in the Bible: centuries later Solomon built the temple at Jerusalem “on Mount Moriah”.

The New Testament remembered the morning as a test of faith. Hebrews says, “By faith, Abraham, being tested, offered up Isaac.” And James, who wrote that God tempts no one, held up this very morning as faith made visible: “Wasn’t Abraham our father justified by works, in that he offered up Isaac his son on the altar?” Whatever James meant in his first chapter, he did not think it ruled out Genesis 22.

The English words had a history of their own. The Wycliffe Bible used an old word for tried. The Geneva Bible said God did prove Abraham. The King James Bible of 1611 chose tempt. English kept moving. Noah Webster’s dictionary of 1828 still gave as the first meaning of awful that which strikes with awe, and noted that common people already used it for frightful. Today many English Bibles say that God tested Abraham, and the World English Bible is one of them.
readings:
Readers have answered the question in several ways, and the answers often overlap.

The first looks at the words. Genesis uses the Hebrew nasah, which Bible Hub’s Hebrew lexicon gives as test, try, prove, tempt, with a warning that tempt is not meant there in the modern sense of the word. The Greek peirazo has the same range. Thayer’s lexicon separates two uses: to entice a person to sin, the sense of James 1:13, and, of God, to send hardship on someone in order to prove his character and the steadfastness of his faith, with Genesis 22:1 among its examples. On this reading James denies the first and Genesis tells of the second.

A second reading looks at the purpose. In James, temptation rises from a person’s own desire and ends in sin and death. The test in Genesis ends with the boy alive and the promise sworn again. Moses used the same language for Israel’s years in the wilderness: God led them “to test you, to know what was in your heart”.

A third reading places the clash mostly in English. When the King James Bible was made, tempt could still mean to put to the test, and a translation that says tested, as the World English Bible does, gives the sense of the Hebrew.

Others say the verb is not the hardest part. Whatever word is used, Genesis has God ask a father for his son. Søren Kierkegaard saw in Abraham the height of faith, and others, such as Francis Schaeffer, have argued with how he read it.
argued:
Christian readers set the two verses side by side long before there was an English Bible. A note printed with the Latin Vulgate at Genesis 22:1 passes on what Augustine of Hippo wrote in his questions on Genesis: James says that God tempts no one, but James is speaking of the temptation by which a person is entangled in sin. In his City of God Augustine kept the old word and said what Abraham’s test was for: [[augustine]]

John Calvin, in his commentary on Genesis, put James 1:13 right beside this verse. James, he wrote, was answering people who tried to lay the blame for their own sins on God, and that did not stop God from testing Abraham in his own way. On the same scene in Hebrews 11 he put it in one line: [[calvin]]

Two centuries after the King James Bible, Noah Webster’s American dictionary of 1828 sorted the two verses in its own way. It put the line from James under the first sense of tempt, to entice to something wrong, and Genesis 22:1 under the fifth: [[webster]]

In these pages none of the three sets Genesis against James. Calvin’s quarrel was with readers who used words like these to lay their own sins at God’s door.
point: Set back in their own chapters, the two verses speak of two different things under one old word. Genesis tells of a test that God gave to prove a man’s faith, and it ended with the son alive. James speaks of the pull toward evil that rises from a person’s own desire, and says God is never its source. James himself saw no conflict: he held up Abraham on that mountain as faith shown in what he did.
lesson:
There is a difference between being tested and being tempted, and it can change how you read your own life.

Some of what you face may be hard without being a trap: a loss, a long wait, a choice that costs you something you love. Abraham waited twenty-five years for a son and was then asked to give him back. Genesis does not pretend that was easy, and you do not have to pretend your hard things are easy either. James even calls such trials a reason for joy, because the testing of faith produces endurance.

Temptation is something else. James is plain about where it comes from: not from God, but from what pulls inside us. When you feel that pull, you do not need to wonder whether God set it there. You can bring it to him and ask for help.

If you are in a hard season, you could read Genesis 22 slowly, then James 1, and ask for the wisdom James says God gives, the God “who gives to all liberally and without reproach”. And if you do not share this faith, the passage still holds something worth keeping: a hard season can show what is in a person without being meant to break them.

echoes.note: Moses tells Israel that God led them through the wilderness “to test you, to know what was in your heart”. A test that brings the heart to light, the kind Abraham faced on the mountain.
Peter’s letter calls faith under trial “more precious than gold that perishes”. A trial is not meant to destroy faith but to show what it is worth.
Temptation is real, but Paul does not make God its author either. He says “God is faithful”, sets its limit and will “make the way of escape”.
